newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: "Mine's a cuppa," says rescued British sailor.
newsitem.headline: "Mine's a cuppa," says rescued British sailor.

text.p: British solo sailor Tony Bullimore thanked God on Thursday after surviving five days in the icy Southern Ocean and then asked his rescuers for a cup of tea.

"Some of his first words were 'Thank God' and 'It's a miracle' and when we got him back in the boat he said he wouldn't mind a cup of tea," Captain Raydon Gates, commander of the frigate Adelaide which led the rescue, told Reuters.
A 56-year-old described as a former Royal Marine, Bullimore capsized on Sunday as he was racing between Australia and the Antarctic in the Vendee Globe round-the-world race.
He spent five days trapped in his upturned hull and was rescued only a few hours after fellow competitor Thierry Dubois of France.
Gates said Bullimore was dehydrated, suffering from mild hypothermia and had lost the top of a frostbitten finger in an accident two days ago, but he was otherwise in good spirits.
"Miracle is probably the word that pops to mind. It was just so thrilling," Gates said of the rescue.
Australian Defence Force spokesman Colonel Andrew Reynolds added: "He's a very tough man, an ex-Royal Marine. Even though he's 56 years old this man is a born survivor.
"He's suffering from exposure but he's in good spirits and I can understand that, we're in good spirits as well having found him alive."

Bullimore's 81-year-old aunt Dinah Twomey, who lives near the West Australian city of Perth where the two rescued sailors were expected to arrive on Monday, seemed unsurprised by her nephew's survival. Twomey has not seen her nephew in 20 years because every time she returns to Britain he is off sailing.
"He's always been a very lucky boy. His yachts have caught fire at sea twice and he's been rescued before. But this really is a miracle," she said.
"He's only a little man, probably not five feet (1.50 metres) tall, but like a lot of little people he's got a lot of character."
